strengths: CogReact addresses a meaningful problem: predicting cognitive responses under changing external feedback. Combining task representations, behavioral calibration, and sequential correction is a well-motivated contribution even though its components are established techniques.

The newly collected dataset of 21,157 arithmetic responses across four feedback conditions is potentially valuable. The manuscript describes the collection procedure, reports ethical approval and consent, and provides a code/data release link.

The reported arithmetic results are promising: numeric-input CogReact achieves MAPE 0.2703 versus 0.3052 for the strongest listed baseline, an approximately 11.4% reduction. The hybrid model also improves over pure DRL in the participant-held-out evaluation.

The evaluation includes multiple input representations, two additional public datasets, component ablations, and neural models incorporating DDM without RL. This breadth provides useful evidence beyond a single favorable comparison.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering interpretable cognitive dynamics is insufficiently supported. Appendix A.7.1 constructs trajectories using a sigmoid, Brownian noise, and an SVC-derived boundary; the connection to human diffusion dynamics is not validated. Optimizing endpoint response-time error cannot uniquely identify intermediate perturbations. Figure 3 even shows nonzero 'time pressure effects' in the None group, consistent with correcting baseline prediction errors. Matching aggregate behavioral trends therefore does not establish the proposed within-trial mechanism.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate the source of improvement. Pure DRL changes the visual encoder, action scaling, temporal resolution, and episode structure simultaneously with removing DDM. The additional DL+DDM comparisons are useful, but predicting DDM parameters does not provide a matched sequential correction control. Feedback-timing ablations and comparisons with established time-varying diffusion models would better establish whether the gains specifically require the proposed temporal mechanism and clarify the advance over prior cognitive modeling.

Important information boundaries remain unclear. Although train/test splits are described, the manuscript does not explicitly establish that all human-fitted SVC/SVR stages and preprocessing are refitted within every split, including LOPO, or identify which unstimulated trials establish baseline performance. For CPC18, alternative-outcome feedback is used to predict response time, but such feedback ordinarily follows the decision. Its temporal alignment must be specified to rule out using information unavailable when the predicted response occurs.

The statistical evidence overstates certainty. Table 4 explicitly labels percentiles of individual prediction errors as confidence intervals; these are not confidence intervals for mean performance. The permutation procedures do not specify whether they preserve pairing and participant-level dependence, despite many repeated observations per person. Confidence intervals for paired performance differences across participants and training runs are needed, particularly for the small general-level hybrid-versus-pure difference of 0.2999 versus 0.3034.

The PeerEdu evaluation does not convincingly establish useful continuous-state prediction. Curiosity lies in [0,1], where MAPE is undefined at zero and highly sensitive to small targets, yet zero handling is unspecified. The reported MAPE of 0.950 is close to the value of 1 obtained by always predicting zero for positive targets. MAE, constant-predictor comparisons, and a clearer justification for mapping curiosity magnitude onto an accumulation-time construction are necessary.

Reproduction remains difficult despite the extensive appendix: the exact sigmoid parameterization, diffusion variance, discount factor, trajectory update, and adaptations for numeric-input CogReact and curiosity are insufficiently specified. Separately, participant counts should be reconciled: Section 3.1 reports 44, Table 2 reports 50, and Appendix A.3.1 leaves 36 after exclusions. These reporting gaps, together with the unresolved evaluation and mechanistic issues, make rejection more appropriate despite the promising prediction results.
